title: IAF Signs Rs 135 Crore Deal With Delhi Startup for Mirage 2000 Simulators
excerpt: Threye Interactive, a NewSpace Research subsidiary founded by former IAF Mirage pilot Sameer Joshi, will deliver VR-based part-task trainers for the fighter fleet after winning an iDEX challenge.
body:
• The Indian Air Force has awarded a contract worth about ₹135 crore (roughly $14 million) to New Delhi startup Threye Interactive for indigenous part-task combat training simulators for the Mirage 2000 fleet. The deal was signed in late September 2026, with the value publicly confirmed on September 30.
  • Threye Interactive, a subsidiary of NewSpace Research & Technologies founded by former IAF Mirage pilot Sameer Joshi, developed the system under the iDEX Defence India Start-up Challenge-5 and has completed IAF trials on the upgraded Mirage 2000.
  • Reader utility: a part-task trainer replicates specific cockpit functions — radar employment, target identification, weapon selection, threat response — so pilots can drill complex sequences repeatedly without burning costly flying hours or airframe life on the four-decade-old fleet.
  • No official Press Information Bureau release has been issued, and the quantity of trainers and delivery schedule have not been disclosed.

Opening news lead

The Indian Air Force has handed a frontline fighter-training contract to a homegrown startup. The service has awarded Threye Interactive, a subsidiary of NewSpace Research & Technologies, a contract valued at about ₹135 crore — roughly $14 million — for indigenous part-task combat training simulators for its Mirage 2000 fleet, defence publication Livefist reported on September 29, with the parent company confirming the value on September 30, 2026.

https://x.com/idrwalerts/status/2105585390598148468

The award moves an iDEX-developed system from prototype to operational training. The trainer, already trialled on the upgraded Mirage 2000, is a compact, PC-based Immersive Flight Training Device that can be configured for individual or group training, in virtual-reality or non-VR modes, according to reporting by SSBCrack.

Context & Background

The system traces back to the Defence India Start-up Challenge-5 (DISC-5) under the Ministry of Defence's Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX) programme, which sought a part-task trainer for the upgraded Mirage 2000 I/TI fleet in the modelling and simulation category. The requirement called for accurate representation of the cockpit — control stick and throttle, multifunction displays, head-up display, function selector and display unit — and the ability to simulate basic flying and the aircraft's existing modes and functions.

Threye's association with the Mirage runs deep. In 2013 the company released Operation Morning Glory, a PC game that put players in a Mirage 2000 on a fictional mission — developed with the involvement of Sameer Joshi, the former IAF fighter pilot who flew the Mirage and later founded NewSpace Research & Technologies. In 2019 the company produced Indian Air Force: A Cut Above, the service's official mobile combat game. This contract is the first time Threye's work will train serving aircrew.

Impact & Analysis

"It shows the IAF trusting an Indian startup with training for a frontline fighter fleet."

— Livefist, on the ₹135-crore contract

At ₹135 crore, the deal is modest next to major fighter and missile programmes. Its significance is institutional: an iDEX challenge winner has crossed the notorious valley between prototype and procurement on a frontline platform. For the IAF, the payoff is operational readiness — a part-task trainer concentrates on specific procedures rather than recreating entire flights, letting pilots rehearse radar use, target identification, weapons selection, and large-force engagements, including scenarios too difficult or expensive to stage in the air.

The Mirage 2000, inducted in the 1980s and upgraded by Dassault Aviation, Thales, and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, was the precision-strike platform of the 1999 Kargil conflict and the 2019 Balakot strike. Preserving flying hours and airframe life on that upgraded fleet while still rehearsing complex mission profiles is the contract's operational logic.

Diaspora Angle

The deal is a data point for diaspora technologists and investors tracking India's defence indigenisation: a startup that began with a Mirage PC game now holds a training contract for the real aircraft. It signals that the iDEX pipeline is producing bankable exits — a case study for Indian-origin engineers and venture capitalists watching the defence-tech corridor.

What's Next / Looking Ahead

Several details remain undisclosed: the number of trainers, their installation locations, and the induction timeline. Threye's separate augmented-reality and virtual-reality technical training system for Mirage 2000 ground personnel — already accepted and deployed by the IAF, per the company — suggests the simulator line could expand to maintenance training as well. Whether Threye's modular architecture extends to other fixed-wing or rotary-wing fleets will be the next signal to watch.
nri_angle: For diaspora technologists and investors, the deal shows India's iDEX pipeline producing bankable exits — a startup that began with a Mirage PC game now holds a real training contract with the IAF.
